Examples and usage
==================

Below you will find short, self-contained snippets that show how to use the most common field
types in real models.  All examples assume the following minimal setup:

.. code-block:: python3

    from tortoise.models import Model
    from tortoise import fields

    # (run Tortoise.init somewhere in your app startup)

--------------------------------------------------------------------
Declaring a model with typical fields
--------------------------------------------------------------------

.. code-block:: python3

    class User(Model):
        id        = fields.IntField(pk=True)          # auto-increment primary key
        username  = fields.CharField(max_length=50, unique=True)
        email     = fields.CharField(max_length=255, null=True)
        is_staff  = fields.BooleanField(default=False)
        joined_at = fields.DatetimeField(auto_now_add=True)
        metadata  = fields.JSONField(default=dict)

    await User.create(username="alice", email="alice@example.com")

--------------------------------------------------------------------
Numeric fields
--------------------------------------------------------------------

``IntField`` (32-bit signed) and ``BigIntField`` (64-bit signed) are the work-horses for
integers.  Both can be auto-incrementing primary keys:

.. code-block:: python3

    class Event(Model):
        id   = fields.BigIntField(pk=True)            # BIGINT AUTO_INCREMENT
        code = fields.IntField(default=0)

``DecimalField`` stores fixed-point numbers with exact precision—ideal for money:

.. code-block:: python3

    class Invoice(Model):
        id      = fields.IntField(pk=True)
        amount  = fields.DecimalField(max_digits=10, decimal_places=2)

    inv = await Invoice.create(amount=Decimal("123.45"))

``FloatField`` is a double-precision floating point when you do not need exact decimals.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
Text and binary data
--------------------------------------------------------------------

``CharField`` is for short, length-limited strings:

.. code-block:: python3

    short = fields.CharField(max_length=120)

``TextField`` is for unbounded text:

.. code-block:: python3

    body = fields.TextField()

``BinaryField`` stores raw bytes:

.. code-block:: python3

    blob = fields.BinaryField()

--------------------------------------------------------------------
Date and time
--------------------------------------------------------------------

.. code-block:: python3

    class Post(Model):
        title      = fields.CharField(max_length=200)
        content    = fields.TextField()
        created_at = fields.DatetimeField(auto_now_add=True)
        updated_at = fields.DatetimeField(auto_now=True)
        pub_date   = fields.DateField(null=True)
        read_time  = fields.TimeDeltaField(null=True)  # stores Python timedelta

    post = await Post.create(title="Hello", content="world")
    print(post.created_at)   # timezone-aware datetime

--------------------------------------------------------------------
UUID and JSON
--------------------------------------------------------------------

Generate a random UUID automatically:

.. code-block:: python3

    class Token(Model):
        key = fields.UUIDField(pk=True, default=uuid.uuid4)
        user = fields.ForeignKeyField("models.User", related_name="tokens")

Store arbitrary JSON structures:

.. code-block:: python3

    cfg = fields.JSONField(default={"theme": "dark", "lang": "en"})

--------------------------------------------------------------------
Enums
--------------------------------------------------------------------

Use ``IntEnumField`` or ``CharEnumField`` to map Python enums to the DB:

.. code-block:: python3

    from enum import IntEnum

    class Status(IntEnum):
        NEW = 1
        DONE = 2

    class Task(Model):
        status = fields.IntEnumField(Status, default=Status.NEW)

--------------------------------------------------------------------
Field options illustrated
--------------------------------------------------------------------

.. code-block:: python3

    class Product(Model):
        sku        = fields.CharField(max_length=20, unique=True, index=True)
        name       = fields.CharField(max_length=100, description="Display name")
        price      = fields.DecimalField(max_digits=8, decimal_places=2, null=True)
        is_active  = fields.BooleanField(default=True)
        created_at = fields.DatetimeField(generated=True)  # DB-side default

--------------------------------------------------------------------
Per-dialect overrides
--------------------------------------------------------------------

Override SQL type or behaviour for a specific database:

.. code-block:: python3

    class MyStringField(fields.CharField):
        max_length = 255

        class _db_postgres:
            SQL_TYPE = "VARCHAR(255)"

        class _db_sqlite:
            SQL_TYPE = "TEXT"

--------------------------------------------------------------------
Computed / generated columns
--------------------------------------------------------------------

Mark a field as ``generated=True`` when the database itself supplies the value
(e.g. auto-increment, PostgreSQL ``GENERATED ALWAYS AS``):

.. code-block:: python3

    class Counter(Model):
        id   = fields.IntField(pk=True, generated=True)  # SERIAL / AUTOINCREMENT
        name = fields.CharField(max_length=50)

--------------------------------------------------------------------
Accessing field metadata at runtime
--------------------------------------------------------------------

.. code-block:: python3

    >>> User._meta.fields_map["username"].describe(serializable=True)
    {
        'name': 'username',
        'field_type': 'CharField',
        'db_column': 'username',
        'db_field_types': {'': 'VARCHAR(50)'},
        'python_type': 'str',
        'generated': False,
        'nullable': False,
        'unique': True,
        'indexed': True,
        'default': None,
        'description': None,
        'docstring': None,
        'constraints': {'maxLength': 50}
    }

These snippets cover the majority of day-to-day patterns when working with Tortoise ORM
fields.

Fields

Usage

Fields are defined as properties of a Model class object:

    from tortoise.models import Model
    from tortoise import fields

    class Tournament(Model):
        id = fields.IntField(pk=True)
        name = fields.CharField(max_length=255)

emphasize-children

Reference

Here is the list of fields available with custom options of these
fields:

Base Field

tortoise.fields.base

Data Fields

tortoise.fields.data

Relational Fields

tortoise.fields.relational

Extending A Field

It is possible to subclass fields allowing use of arbitrary types as
long as they can be represented in a database compatible format. An
example of this would be a simple wrapper around the
~tortoise.fields.CharField to store and query Enum types.

    from enum import Enum
    from typing import Type

    from tortoise import ConfigurationError
    from tortoise.fields import CharField


    class EnumField(CharField):
        """
        An example extension to CharField that serializes Enums
        to and from a str representation in the DB.
        """

        def __init__(self, enum_type: Type[Enum], **kwargs):
            super().__init__(128, **kwargs)
            if not issubclass(enum_type, Enum):
                raise ConfigurationError("{} is not a subclass of Enum!".format(enum_type))
            self._enum_type = enum_type

        def to_db_value(self, value: Enum, instance) -> str:
            return value.value

        def to_python_value(self, value: str) -> Enum:
            try:
                return self._enum_type(value)
            except Exception:
                raise ValueError(
                    "Database value {} does not exist on Enum {}.".format(value, self._enum_type)
                )

When subclassing, make sure that the to_db_value returns the same type
as the superclass (in the case of CharField, that is a str) and that,
naturally, to_python_value accepts the same type in the value parameter
(also str).

.. _models:

Models
======

A **Model** is the single, definitive source of information about your data.  
It contains the essential fields and behaviors of the data you’re storing.  
Tortoise ORM follows the *Active Record* pattern: each model instance is a
row in the database and each model class is a table.

Quick example
-------------

.. code-block:: python3

    from tortoise.models import Model
    from tortoise import fields


    class Tournament(Model):
        """
        A tournament that can host many events.
        """
        id = fields.IntField(pk=True)
        name = fields.CharField(max_length=255)
        created_at = fields.DatetimeField(auto_now_add=True)

        events: fields.ReverseRelation["Event"]

        class Meta:
            table = "tournaments"
            ordering = ["-created_at"]


    class Event(Model):
        """
        An event that belongs to a tournament.
        """
        id = fields.IntField(pk=True)
        name = fields.CharField(max_length=255)
        tournament = fields.ForeignKeyField(
            "models.Tournament", related_name="events"
        )
        participants = fields.ManyToManyField(
            "models.Team", related_name="events", through="event_team"
        )

        class Meta:
            table = "events"


    class Team(Model):
        """
        A team that can participate in many events.
        """
        id = fields.IntField(pk=True)
        name = fields.CharField(max_length=255)

        events: fields.ManyToManyRelation[Event]

        class Meta:
            table = "teams"

Defining a model
----------------

Subclass :class:`tortoise.models.Model` and add
:class:`tortoise.fields.Field` instances as class attributes.

.. code-block:: python3

    from tortoise.models import Model
    from tortoise import fields


    class Author(Model):
        id = fields.IntField(pk=True)
        name = fields.CharField(max_length=50)
        is_active = fields.BooleanField(default=True)

Field types
~~~~~~~~~~~

Tortoise ships with the most common field types:

*   :class:`tortoise.fields.IntField`
*   :class:`tortoise.fields.CharField`
*   :class:`tortoise.fields.TextField`
*   :class:`tortoise.fields.BooleanField`
*   :class:`tortoise.fields.DatetimeField`
*   :class:`tortoise.fields.DateField`
*   :class:`tortoise.fields.DecimalField`
*   :class:`tortoise.fields.FloatField`
*   :class:`tortoise.fields.JSONField`
*   :class:`tortoise.fields.UUIDField`
*   :class:`tortoise.fields.BinaryField`
*   :class:`tortoise.fields.TimeDeltaField`
*   :class:`tortoise.fields.IntEnumField`
*   :class:`tortoise.fields.CharEnumField`

Meta options
~~~~~~~~~~~~

You can control many aspects of the generated table by defining an inner
``Meta`` class:

.. code-block:: python3

    class MyModel(Model):
        ...

        class Meta:
            table = "custom_table_name"
            unique_together = (("field1", "field2"),)
            indexes = (("field1", "field2"),)
            ordering = ["-created_at"]
            app = "my_app"
            table_description = "Stores my data"

abstract
    If ``True`` this model is an *abstract base class* – no table is created.

table
    Database table name.  Defaults to the class name in snake_case.

unique_together
    A tuple of field names that must be unique together.

indexes
    A tuple of tuples, each containing field names to create composite indexes.

ordering
    Default ordering used by ``QuerySet`` when no explicit order is given.

app
    The app label this model belongs to.  Used for migrations.

table_description
    Optional description stored in the database (if the backend supports it).

pk_attr
    Override the name of the primary key attribute (rarely needed).

Primary keys
~~~~~~~~~~~~

By default Tortoise adds an ``id`` :class:`tortoise.fields.IntField`
primary key.  You can override it:

.. code-block:: python3

    class UUIDModel(Model):
        uuid = fields.UUIDField(pk=True)

Relationships
-------------

ForeignKey
~~~~~~~~~~

.. code-block:: python3

    class Post(Model):
        ...
        author = fields.ForeignKeyField("models.User", related_name="posts")

Reverse access is automatically available:

.. code-block:: python3

    user = await User.get(id=1)
    posts = await user.posts.all()

ManyToManyField
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

.. code-block:: python3

    class Student(Model):
        ...
        courses = fields.ManyToManyField(
            "models.Course", related_name="students", through="student_course"
        )

OneToOneField
~~~~~~~~~~~~~

.. code-block:: python3

    class Profile(Model):
        ...
        user = fields.OneToOneField("models.User", related_name="profile")

Reverse relations
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

For every forward relation a reverse relation is created on the related
model.  The name is controlled by ``related_name`` (defaults to
``<model>_set``).

Querying
--------

Each model exposes a rich API for building queries:

.. code-block:: python3

    # Get one
    tournament = await Tournament.get(id=1)

    # Filter
    events = await Event.filter(tournament__name__icontains="chess")

    # Create
    event = await Event.create(name="Final", tournament=tournament)

    # Update
    await Event.filter(id=1).update(name="Grand Final")

    # Delete
    await Event.filter(id=1).delete()

    # Aggregations
    count = await Event.filter(tournament=tournament).count()

    # Prefetch related
    tournaments = (
        await Tournament.all()
        .prefetch_related("events__participants")
    )

Model methods
-------------

save()
~~~~~~

.. code-block:: python3

    author = Author(name="Guido")
    await author.save()  # INSERT
    author.name = "Guido van Rossum"
    await author.save()  # UPDATE

delete()
~~~~~~~~

.. code-block:: python3

    await author.delete()

refresh_from_db()
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

Reload the instance from the database:

.. code-block:: python3

    await author.refresh_from_db()

to_dict()
~~~~~~~~~

Convert the model instance to a plain Python dict:

.. code-block:: python3

    data = await author.to_dict()

Signals
-------

Tortoise emits signals on certain actions.  You can connect receivers:

.. code-block:: python3

    from tortoise.signals import post_save
    from tortoise import models

    @post_save(models.Author)
    async def send_welcome_email(
        sender: Type[models.Author],
        instance: models.Author,
        created: bool,
        using_db,
        update_fields,
    ):
        if created:
            await mailer.send_welcome(instance.email)

Available signals:

*   ``pre_save`` / ``post_save``
*   ``pre_delete`` / ``post_delete``

Transactions
------------

Use the ``in_transaction`` context manager to run code in a transaction:

.. code-block:: python3

    from tortoise.transactions import in_transaction

    async with in_transaction():
        tournament = await Tournament.create(name="New")
        await Event.create(name="Round 1", tournament=tournament)

You can also specify the connection name:

.. code-block:: python3

    async with in_transaction("secondary"):
        ...

Custom managers
---------------

You can add custom query methods by subclassing ``QuerySet`` and assigning
it to the model:

.. code-block:: python3

    class ActiveQuerySet(QuerySet):
        def active(self):
            return self.filter(is_active=True)

    class Author(Model):
        ...
        objects = ActiveQuerySet()

    active_authors = await Author.objects.active()

Indexes & constraints
---------------------

Unique constraints
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

.. code-block:: python3

    class Meta:
        unique_together = (("first_name", "last_name"),)

Database indexes
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

.. code-block:: python3

    class Meta:
        indexes = (
            ("first_name", "last_name"),
            ("email",),
        )

Field validation
----------------

Tortoise validates data before saving:

.. code-block:: python3

    try:
        await Author.create(name=None)  # raises ValidationError
    except IntegrityError:
        ...

Custom fields
-------------

You can create custom fields by subclassing :class:`tortoise.fields.Field`
and implementing ``to_db_value`` and ``to_python_value``.

.. code-block:: python3

    class ColorField(fields.CharField):
        def to_db_value(self, value, instance):
            return value.hex if value else None

        def to_python_value(self, value):
            return Color(value) if value else None

Abstract base classes
---------------------

Define common fields in an abstract model:

.. code-block:: python3

    class TimestampedModel(Model):
        created_at = fields.DatetimeField(auto_now_add=True)
        updated_at = fields.DatetimeField(auto_now=True)

        class Meta:
            abstract = True

    class Post(TimestampedModel):
        title = fields.CharField(max_length=255)

Multiple databases
------------------

Specify the connection per model:

.. code-block:: python3

    class Meta:
        default_connection = "secondary"

API reference
-------------

.. autoclass:: tortoise.models.Model
    :members:
    :undoc-members:
    :exclude-members: Meta, Query

.. autoclass:: tortoise.models.MetaInfo
    :members
results.reference:
Models

Usage

To get working with models, first you should import them

    from tortoise.models import Model

With that you can start describing your own models like that

    class Tournament(Model):
        id = fields.IntField(pk=True)
        name = fields.TextField()
        created = fields.DatetimeField(auto_now_add=True)

        def __str__(self):
            return self.name


    class Event(Model):
        id = fields.IntField(pk=True)
        name = fields.TextField()
        tournament = fields.ForeignKeyField('models.Tournament', related_name='events')
        participants = fields.ManyToManyField('models.Team', related_name='events', through='event_team')
        modified = fields.DatetimeField(auto_now=True)
        prize = fields.DecimalField(max_digits=10, decimal_places=2, null=True)

        def __str__(self):
            return self.name


    class Team(Model):
        id = fields.IntField(pk=True)
        name = fields.TextField()

        def __str__(self):
            return self.name

Let see in details what we accomplished here:

    class Tournament(Model):

Every model should be derived from base model. You also can derive from
your own model subclasses and you can make abstract models like this

    class AbstractTournament(Model):
        id = fields.IntField(pk=True)
        name = fields.TextField()
        created = fields.DatetimeField(auto_now_add=True)

        class Meta:
            abstract = True

        def __str__(self):
            return self.name

This models won't be created in schema generation and won't create
relations to other models.

Further we have field fields.DatetimeField(auto_now=True). Options
auto_now and auto_now_add work like Django's options.

Use of __models__

If you define the variable __models__ in the module which you load your
models from, generate_schema will use that list, rather than
automatically finding models for you.

Primary Keys

In Tortoise ORM we require that a model has a primary key.

That primary key will be accessible through a reserved field pk which
will be an alias of whichever field has been nominated as a primary key.
That alias field can be used as a field name when doing filtering e.g.
.filter(pk=...) etc…

Note

We currently support single (non-composite) primary keys of any
indexable field type, but only these field types are recommended:

    IntField
    BigIntField
    CharField
    UUIDField

One must define a primary key by setting a pk parameter to True. If you
don't define a primary key, we will create a primary key of type
IntField with name of id for you.

Note

If this is used on an Integer Field, generated will be set to True
unless you explicitly pass generated=False as well.

Any of these are valid primary key definitions in a Model:

    id = fields.IntField(pk=True)

    checksum = fields.CharField(pk=True)

    guid = fields.UUIDField(pk=True)

Inheritance

When defining models in Tortoise ORM, you can save a lot of repetitive
work by leveraging from inheritance.

You can define fields in more generic classes and they are automatically
available in derived classes. Base classes are not limited to Model
classes. Any class will work. This way you are able to define your
models in a natural and easy to maintain way.

Let's have a look at some examples.

    from tortoise import fields
    from tortoise.models import Model

    class TimestampMixin():
        created_at = fields.DatetimeField(null=True, auto_now_add=True)
        modified_at = fields.DatetimeField(null=True, auto_now=True)

    class NameMixin():
        name = fields.CharField(40, unique=True)

    class MyAbstractBaseModel(Model):
        id = fields.IntField(pk=True)

        class Meta:
            abstract = True

    class UserModel(TimestampMixin, MyAbstractBaseModel):
        # Overriding the id definition
        # from MyAbstractBaseModel
        id = fields.UUIDField(pk=True)

        # Adding additional fields
        first_name = fields.CharField(20, null=True)

        class Meta:
            table = "user"


    class RoleModel(TimestampMixin, NameMixin, MyAbstractBaseModel):

        class Meta:
            table = "role"

Using the Meta class is not necessary. But it is a good habit, to give
your table an explicit name. This way you can change the model name
without breaking the schema. So the following definition is valid.

    class RoleModel(TimestampMixin, NameMixin, MyAbstractBaseModel):
        pass

ForeignKeyField

    tournament = fields.ForeignKeyField('models.Tournament', related_name='events')
    participants = fields.ManyToManyField('models.Team', related_name='events')
    modified = fields.DatetimeField(auto_now=True)
    prize = fields.DecimalField(max_digits=10, decimal_places=2, null=True)

In event model we got some more fields, that could be interesting for
us.

fields.ForeignKeyField('models.Tournament', related_name='events')

    Here we create foreign key reference to tournament. We create it by
    referring to model by it's literal, consisting of app name and model
    name. models is default app name, but you can change it in
    class Meta with app = 'other'.

related_name

    Is keyword argument, that defines field for related query on
    referenced models, so with that you could fetch all tournaments's
    events with like this:

The DB-backing field

Note

A ForeignKeyField is a virtual field, meaning it has no direct DB
backing. Instead it has a field (by default called {FKNAME}_id (that is,
just an _id is appended) that is the actual DB-backing field.

It will just contain the Key value of the related table.

This is an important detail as it would allow one to assign/read the
actual value directly, which could be considered an optimization if the
entire foreign object isn't needed.

Specifying an FK can be done via either passing the object:

    await SomeModel.create(tournament=the_tournament)
    # or
    somemodel.tournament=the_tournament

or by directly accessing the DB-backing field:

    await SomeModel.create(tournament_id=the_tournament.pk)
    # or
    somemodel.tournament_id=the_tournament.pk

Querying a relationship is typicall done by appending a double
underscore, and then the foreign object's field. Then a normal query
attr can be appended. This can be chained if the next key is also a
foreign object:

  {FKNAME}__{FOREIGNFIELD}__gt=3

  or

  {FKNAME}__{FOREIGNFK}__{VERYFOREIGNFIELD}__gt=3

There is however one major limiatation. We don't want to restrict
foreign column names, or have ambiguity (e.g. a foreign object may have
a field called isnull)

Then this would be entierly ambugious:

  {FKNAME}__isnull

To prevent that we require that direct filters be applied to the
DB-backing field of the foreign key:

  {FKNAME}_id__isnull

Fetching the foreign object

Fetching foreign keys can be done with both async and sync interfaces.

Async fetch:

    events = await tournament.events.all()

You can async iterate over it like this:

    async for event in tournament.events:
        ...

Sync usage requires that you call fetch_related before the time, and
then you can use common functions such as:

    await tournament.fetch_related('events')
    events = list(tournament.events)
    eventlen = len(tournament.events)
    if SomeEvent in tournament.events:
        ...
    if tournament.events:
        ...
    firstevent = tournament.events[0]

To get the Reverse-FK, e.g. an event.tournament we currently only
support the sync interface.

    await event.fetch_related('tournament')
    tournament = event.tournament

ManyToManyField

Next field is
fields.ManyToManyField('models.Team', related_name='events'). It
describes many to many relation to model Team.

To add to a ManyToManyField both the models need to be saved, else you
will get an OperationalError raised.

Resolving many to many fields can be done with both async and sync
interfaces.

Async fetch:

    participants = await tournament.participants.all()

You can async iterate over it like this:

    async for participant in tournament.participants:
        ...

Sync usage requires that you call fetch_related before the time, and
then you can use common functions such as:

    await tournament.fetch_related('participants')
    participants = list(tournament.participants)
    participantlen = len(tournament.participants)
    if SomeParticipant in tournament.participants:
        ...
    if tournament.participants:
        ...
    firstparticipant = tournament.participants[0]

The reverse lookup of team.event_team works exactly the same way.

Improving relational type hinting

Since Tortoise ORM is still a young project, it does not have such
widespread support by various editors who help you writing code using
good autocomplete for models and different relations between them.
However, you can get such autocomplete by doing a little work yourself.
All you need to do is add a few annotations to your models for fields
that are responsible for the relations.

Here is an updated example from getting_started, that will add
autocomplete for all models including fields for the relations between
models.

    from tortoise.models import Model
    from tortoise import fields


    class Tournament(Model):
        id = fields.IntField(pk=True)
        name = fields.CharField(max_length=255)

        events: fields.ReverseRelation["Event"]

        def __str__(self):
            return self.name


    class Event(Model):
        id = fields.IntField(pk=True)
        name = fields.CharField(max_length=255)
        tournament: fields.ForeignKeyRelation[Tournament] = fields.ForeignKeyField(
            "models.Tournament", related_name="events"
        )
        participants: fields.ManyToManyRelation["Team"] = fields.ManyToManyField(
            "models.Team", related_name="events", through="event_team"
        )

        def __str__(self):
            return self.name


    class Team(Model):
        id = fields.IntField(pk=True)
        name = fields.CharField(max_length=255)

        events: fields.ManyToManyRelation[Event]

        def __str__(self):
            return self.name

.. _pydantic:

How to generate Pydantic Models from Tortoise Models
==================================================

Tortoise ORM ships with a small helper library that can automatically create
`Pydantic <https://pydantic-docs.helpmanual.io/>`_ models from your Tortoise
models.  This is useful when you want to expose your data through a REST API
or validate incoming payloads without duplicating model definitions.

The helper is located in ``tortoise.contrib.pydantic`` and exposes two public
functions:

* ``pydantic_model_creator`` – generates a *single* Pydantic model for one
  Tortoise model instance.
* ``pydantic_queryset_creator`` – generates a *list* Pydantic model that wraps
  the above in ``List[...]`` (handy for serialising query-sets).

Both functions inspect the Tortoise model at runtime, respect all declared
fields, relations, and constraints, and can be fine-tuned through either
function arguments or a nested ``PydanticMeta`` class.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1.  Minimal example
--------------------------------------------------------------------

.. code-block:: python3

    from tortoise.models import Model
    from tortoise import fields
    from tortoise.contrib.pydantic import pydantic_model_creator


    class User(Model):
        id = fields.IntField(pk=True)
        name = fields.CharField(max_length=50)
        email = fields.CharField(max_length=255, unique=True)
        is_active = fields.BooleanField(default=True)

        class PydanticMeta:
            exclude = ("is_active",)      # do not expose internal flag


    User_Pydantic = pydantic_model_creator(User)

The resulting ``User_Pydantic`` is a normal Pydantic model:

.. code-block:: pycon

    >>> await User.create(name="Alice", email="alice@example.com")
    >>> user = await User_Pydantic.from_tortoise_orm(await User.get(id=1))
    >>> user.json()
    '{"id": 1, "name": "Alice", "email": "alice@example.com"}'

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2.  Controlling the generated schema
--------------------------------------------------------------------

You can influence the schema in three different ways:

A.  Function arguments  
    All options can be supplied directly when calling the creator:

    .. code-block:: python3

        User_Pydantic = pydantic_model_creator(
            User,
            exclude=("email",),
            computed=("full_name",),
            allow_cycles=False,
            sort_alphabetically=True,
        )

B.  ``PydanticMeta`` class  
    Place an inner class named ``PydanticMeta`` on the Tortoise model to set
    project-wide defaults:

    .. code-block:: python3

        class User(Model):
            ...

            class PydanticMeta:
                exclude = ("password_hash",)
                computed = ("full_name",)
                max_recursion = 2
                backward_relations = False

C.  Mixing both  
    Arguments passed to the creator always override the values defined in
    ``PydanticMeta``.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3.  Reference – ``PydanticMeta`` options
--------------------------------------------------------------------

``include``  
    Tuple of field names.  If non-empty, **only** these fields will appear in
    the Pydantic model.

``exclude``  
    Tuple of field names to omit from the schema.

``computed``  
    Tuple of *methods* on the model that should be exposed as read-only
    computed fields.

``backward_relations`` *(default: True)*  
    Whether to automatically include reverse FK and M2M relations.  Disable
    when the resulting payload can become too large.

``max_recursion`` *(default: 3)*  
    How deep the generator will follow nested relations before truncating the
    branch.

``allow_cycles`` *(default: False)*  
    Allow self-referencing or circular relations.  Use with care – the
    resulting JSON can explode in size.

``exclude_raw_fields`` *(default: True)*  
    Remove the raw ``_id`` columns that Tortoise uses internally for foreign
    keys.

``sort_alphabetically`` *(default: False)*  
    Sort fields by name instead of declaration order.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
4.  Handling relations
--------------------------------------------------------------------

Forward relations (FK, O2O) are embedded as nested Pydantic models.  
Reverse relations (backward FK, M2O, M2M) become **lists** of nested models.

Example:

.. code-block:: python3

    class Team(Model):
        id = fields.IntField(pk=True)
        name = fields.CharField(max_length=50)
        members = fields.ManyToManyField("models.User", related_name="teams")

    Team_Pydantic = pydantic_model_creator(Team)
    User_Pydantic = pydantic_model_creator(User)

    >>> team = await Team.create(name="A-Team")
    >>> await team.members.add(await User.create(name="Alice", email="a@t.com"))
    >>> await Team_Pydantic.from_tortoise_orm(team)
    {"id": 1, "name": "A-Team", "members": [{"id": 1, "name": "Alice", "email": "a@t.com"}]}

Recursion is automatically limited by ``max_recursion``.  Increase it or set
``allow_cycles=True`` when you really need deep nesting.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
5.  Computed fields
--------------------------------------------------------------------

Any method that takes only ``self`` and returns JSON-serialisable data can be
listed in ``computed``:

.. code-block:: python3

    class User(Model):
        first_name = fields.CharField(max_length=50)
        last_name  = fields.CharField(max_length=50)

        class PydanticMeta:
            computed = ("full_name",)

        def full_name(self) -> str:
            return f"{self.first_name} {self.last_name}"

The method is called during serialisation and its result is exposed under the
same name.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
6.  Generating list schemas
--------------------------------------------------------------------

Use ``pydantic_queryset_creator`` when you need to serialise an entire
query-set:

.. code-block:: python3

    from tortoise.contrib.pydantic import pydantic_queryset_creator

    UserList_Pydantic = pydantic_queryset_creator(User)

    >>> users = await User.all()
    >>> await UserList_Pydantic.from_queryset(users)
    [{"id": 1, "name": "Alice", ...}, {"id": 2, "name": "Bob", ...}]

The list model is simply ``List[User_Pydantic]`` with an auto-generated name
(``UserList`` by default).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
7.  Read-only / write-only fields
--------------------------------------------------------------------

Tortoise field options such as ``readOnly=True`` (e.g. auto-now timestamps)
are honoured.  If you need a *write-only* schema (e.g. for POST bodies) pass
``exclude_readonly=True``:

.. code-block:: python3

    UserIn_Pydantic = pydantic_model_creator(User, exclude_readonly=True)

All primary keys, auto timestamps, and any field marked ``readOnly`` will be
removed from the schema.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
8.  Caching & uniqueness
--------------------------------------------------------------------

The generator caches every unique schema under a deterministic name.  Calling
the creator twice with identical parameters returns the same class object,
avoiding duplicate definitions and keeping memory usage low.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
9.  Summary
--------------------------------------------------------------------

* Import ``pydantic_model_creator`` or ``pydantic_queryset_creator`` from
  ``tortoise.contrib.pydantic``.
* Optionally add a ``PydanticMeta`` inner class to your Tortoise model.
* Call the creator once at import time and reuse the resulting Pydantic model
  everywhere you need serialisation or validation.

With these few lines you get fully typed, validated, and documented Pydantic
schemas that always stay in sync with your database models.

How to use QuerySet to build your queries
========================================

The ``QuerySet`` is the main tool you use to fetch data from the database.  
It is **lazy**: nothing is sent to the database until you explicitly ask for the
results (by iterating, awaiting, calling ``.first()``, ``.count()``, …).

Creating a QuerySet
-------------------

Every model class exposes at least one QuerySet through its manager:

.. code-block:: python3

    from models import User

    # All users
    qs = User.all()          # identical to User.objects

    # or start from scratch
    qs = User.filter(is_active=True)

Filtering
---------

``filter(**lookups)`` and ``exclude(**lookups)``
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

.. code-block:: python3

    # Users whose name starts with "A"
    User.filter(name__startswith="A")

    # Exclude staff
    User.exclude(is_staff=True)

You can traverse relations with double underscores:

.. code-block:: python3

    # Events whose tournament's name is "Champions"
    Event.filter(tournament__name="Champions")

Complex predicates with ``Q`` objects
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

.. code-block:: python3

    from tortoise.query_utils import Q

    User.filter(
        Q(is_staff=True) | Q(is_superuser=True),
        ~Q(status="blocked")
    )

Ordering
--------

.. code-block:: python3

    User.order_by("last_name", "-date_joined")

    # Order by related field
    Event.order_by("tournament__name", "-name")

Limit & offset
--------------

.. code-block:: python3

    # Pagination
    Event.offset(20).limit(10)

Selecting only what you need
----------------------------

``values(*fields)`` returns dictionaries:

.. code-block:: python3

    User.filter(is_staff=True).values("id", "username")

``values_list(*fields, flat=False)`` returns tuples (or a flat list):

.. code-block:: python3

    User.values_list("id", flat=True)   # [1, 2, 3, …]

Distinct rows
-------------

.. code-block:: python3

    User.values("country").distinct()

Annotations & database functions
--------------------------------

Use ``annotate(**{alias: Function})`` to add computed columns:

.. code-block:: python3

    from tortoise.functions import Count, Sum

    # Number of events per tournament
    Tournament.annotate(event_count=Count("events"))

    # Total prize money per user
    User.annotate(total_prize=Sum("wins__prize"))

Filtering on annotations works automatically:

.. code-block:: python3

    Tournament.annotate(event_count=Count("events")).filter(event_count__gte=5)

Grouping
--------

Combine ``group_by`` with ``values``/``values_list``:

.. code-block:: python3

    Event.group_by("tournament_id").annotate(
        avg_prize=Avg("prize")
    ).values("tournament_id", "avg_prize")

Prefetching related objects
---------------------------

Avoid the N+1 problem by pre-loading relations:

.. code-block:: python3

    tournaments = await Tournament.all().prefetch_related("events", "events__participants")

You can fine-tune the prefetched QuerySet:

.. code-block:: python3

    from tortoise.query_utils import Prefetch

    User.prefetch_related(
        Prefetch("events", queryset=Event.filter(status="finished"))
    )

Single-object queries
---------------------

``get(**lookup)`` returns exactly one object or raises:

.. code-block:: python3

    user = await User.get(id=42)

``first()`` returns the first match or ``None``:

.. code-block:: python3

    top = await Event.order_by("-score").first()

``get_or_none()``, ``update_or_create()``, etc. are also available.

Counting
--------

.. code-block:: python3

    total = await User.filter(is_active=True).count()

Exists check
------------

.. code-block:: python3

    if await User.filter(email=email).exists():
        ...

Deleting & updating in bulk
---------------------------

.. code-block:: python3

    await User.filter(is_active=False).delete()
    await User.filter(country="US").update(currency="USD")

Raw SQL fragments
-----------------

When you need database-specific expressions you can pass raw terms:

.. code-block:: python3

    from pypika.terms import Term

    User.annotate(
        full_name=Term("CONCAT(first_name, ' ', last_name)")
    )

Chaining everything together
----------------------------

QuerySets are immutable; every call returns a new instance, so you can safely
chain and reuse them:

.. code-block:: python3

    base_qs = Event.filter(status="published")

    recent = base_qs.order_by("-created_at").limit(10)
    old    = base_qs.order_by("created_at").limit(10)

    # Both queries are independent

Asynchronous iteration
----------------------

.. code-block:: python3

    async for user in User.filter(is_active=True):
        ...

Remember: until you **await** or iterate, no SQL is executed.
results.reference:
Query API

This document describes how to use QuerySet to build your queries

Be sure to check examples for better understanding

You start your query from your model class:

    Event.filter(id=1)

There are several method on model itself to start query:

-   filter(*args, **kwargs) - create QuerySet with given filters
-   exclude(*args, **kwargs) - create QuerySet with given excluding
    filters
-   all() - create QuerySet without filters
-   first() - create QuerySet limited to one object and returning
    instance instead of list
-   annotate() - create QuerySet with given annotation

This method returns QuerySet object, that allows further filtering and
some more complex operations

Also model class have this methods to create object:

-   create(**kwargs) - creates object with given kwargs
-   get_or_create(defaults, **kwargs) - gets object for given kwargs, if
    not found create it with additional kwargs from defaults dict

Also instance of model itself has these methods:

-   save() - update instance, or insert it, if it was never saved before
-   delete() - delete instance from db
-   fetch_related(*args) - fetches objects related to instance. It can
    fetch FK relation, Backward-FK relations and M2M relations. It also
    can fetch variable depth of related objects like this:
    await team.fetch_related('events__tournament') - this will fetch all
    events for team, and for each of this events their tournament will
    be prefetched too. After fetching objects they should be available
    normally like this: team.events[0].tournament.name

Another approach to work with related objects on instance is to query
them explicitly in async for:

    async for team in event.participants:
        print(team.name)

You also can filter related objects like this:

    await team.events.filter(name='First')

which will return you a QuerySet object with predefined filter

QuerySet

QuerySet could be constructed, filtered and passed around without
actually hitting database. Only after you await QuerySet, it will
generate query and run it against database.

Here are some common usage scenarios with QuerySet (we are using models
defined in getting_started):

Regular select into model instances:

    await Event.filter(name__startswith='FIFA')

This query will get you all events with name starting with FIFA, where
name is fields defined on model, and startswith is filter modifier. Take
note, that modifiers should be separated by double underscore. You can
read more on filter modifiers in Filtering section of this document.

It's also possible to filter your queries with .exclude():

    await Team.exclude(name__icontains='junior')

As more interesting case, when you are working with related data, you
could also build your query around related entities:

    # getting all events, which tournament name is "World Cup"
    await Event.filter(tournament__name='World Cup')

    # Gets all teams participating in events with ids 1, 2, 3
    await Team.filter(events__id__in=[1,2,3])

    # Gets all tournaments where teams with "junior" in their name are participating
    await Tournament.filter(event__participants__name__icontains='junior').distinct()

Usually you not only want to filter by related data, but also get that
related data as well. You could do it using .prefetch_related():

    # This will fetch events, and for each of events ``.tournament`` field will be populated with
    # corresponding ``Tournament`` instance
    await Event.all().prefetch_related('tournament')

    # This will fetch tournament with their events and teams for each event
    tournament_list = await Tournament.all().prefetch_related('events__participants')

    # Fetched result for m2m and backward fk relations are stored in list-like container
    for tournament in tournament_list:
        print([e.name for e in tournament.events])

General rule about how prefetch_related() works is that each level of
depth of related models produces 1 additional query, so
.prefetch_related('events__participants') will produce two additional
queries to fetch your data.

Sometimes, when performance is crucial, you don't want to make
additional queries like this. In cases like this you could use values()
or values_list() to produce more efficient query

    # This will return list of dicts with keys 'id', 'name', 'tournament_name' and
    # 'tournament_name' will be populated by name of related tournament.
    # And it will be done in one query
    events = await Event.filter(id__in=[1,2,3]).values('id', 'name', tournament_name='tournament__name')

QuerySet also supports aggregation and database functions through
.annotate() method

    from tortoise.functions import Count, Trim, Lower, Upper, Coalesce

    # This query will fetch all tournaments with 10 or more events, and will
    # populate filed `.events_count` on instances with corresponding value
    await Tournament.annotate(events_count=Count('events')).filter(events_count__gte=10)
    await Tournament.annotate(clean_name=Trim('name'))).filter(clean_name='tournament')
    await Tournament.annotate(name_upper=Upper('name'))).filter(name_upper='TOURNAMENT')
    await Tournament.annotate(name_lower=Lower('name'))).filter(name_lower='tournament')
    await Tournament.annotate(desc_clean=Coalesce('desc', ''))).filter(desc_clean='')

Q objects

Sometimes you need to do more complicated queries than the simple AND
<model>.filter() provides. Luckily we have Q objects to spice things up
and help you find what you need. These Q-objects can then be used as
argument to <model>.filter() instead.

Q objects are extremely versatile, some example use cases:

    -   creating an OR filter
    -   nested filters
    -   inverted filters
    -   combining any of the above to simply write complicated
        multilayer filters

Q objects can take any (special) kwargs for filtering that
<model>.filter() accepts, see those docs for a full list of filter
options in that regard.

They can also be combined by using bitwise operators (| is OR and & is
AND for those unfamiliar with bitwise operators)

For example to find the events with as name Event 1 or Event 2:

    found_events = await Event.filter(
        Q(name='Event 1') | Q(name='Event 2')
    )

Q objects can be nested as well, the above for example is equivalent to:

    found_events = await Event.filter(
        Q(Q(name='Event 1'), Q(name='Event 2'), join_type="OR")
    )

If join type is omitted it defaults to AND.

Note

Q objects without filter arguments are considered NOP and will be
ignored for the final query (regardless on if they are used as AND or OR
param)

Also, Q objects support negated to generate NOT (~ operator) clause in
your query

    not_third_events = await Event.filter(~Q(name='3'))

tortoise.query_utils

Filtering

When using .filter() method you can use number of modifiers to field
names to specify desired operation

    teams = await Team.filter(name__icontains='CON')

-   not
-   in - checks if value of field is in passed list
-   not_in
-   gte - greater or equals than passed value
-   gt - greater than passed value
-   lte - lower or equals than passed value
-   lt - lower than passed value
-   range - between and given two values
-   isnull - field is null
-   not_isnull - field is not null
-   contains - field contains specified substring
-   icontains - case insensitive contains
-   startswith - if field starts with value
-   istartswith - case insensitive startswith
-   endswith - if field ends with value
-   iendswith - case insensitive endswith
-   iequals - case insensitive equals

Complex prefetch

Sometimes it is required to fetch only certain related records. You can
achieve it with Prefetch object:

    tournament_with_filtered = await Tournament.all().prefetch_related(
        Prefetch('events', queryset=Event.filter(name='First'))
    ).first()

F expression

An F() object represents the value of a model field. It makes it
possible to refer to model field values and perform database operations
using them without actually having to pull them out of the database into
Python memory.

For example to use F to update user balance atomic:

    from tortoise.expressions import F
    await User.filter(id=1).update(balance = F('balance') - 10)
    await User.filter(id=1).update(balance = F('balance') + F('award'), award = 0)

    # or use .save()
    user = await User.get(id=1)
    user.balance = F('balance') - 10
    await user.save(update_fields=['balance'])

How to generate schema
======================

Tortoise ORM can create the complete SQL DDL (tables, indexes, etc.) that matches your declared models.  
There are two supported ways to obtain or apply the schema:

1. **Generate the SQL text only** – useful for migrations, code reviews, or manual execution.
2. **Generate and execute the SQL immediately** – useful during development or in automated tests.

Both approaches are driven by the same helper functions and respect the same safety flag.

--------------------------------------------------
Generating the SQL text
--------------------------------------------------

.. code-block:: python

    from tortoise import Tortoise
    from tortoise.utils import get_schema_sql

    await Tortoise.init(
        db_url="sqlite://db.sqlite3",
        modules={"models": ["my_project.models"]}
    )

    sql = get_schema_sql(Tortoise.get_connection("default"), safe=True)
    print(sql)

``get_schema_sql(client, safe)``
    * ``client`` – an active ``BaseDBAsyncClient`` instance (obtained from ``Tortoise.get_connection(...)`` after ``Tortoise.init``).
    * ``safe`` – when ``True`` each ``CREATE TABLE`` statement is wrapped in an ``IF NOT EXISTS`` clause, preventing errors if the table already exists.

The function returns the complete DDL string for all registered models.

--------------------------------------------------
Generating and applying the schema
--------------------------------------------------

.. code-block:: python

    from tortoise import Tortoise
    from tortoise.utils import generate_schema_for_client

    await Tortoise.init(
        db_url="postgres://user:pass@localhost:5432/mydb",
        modules={"models": ["my_project.models"]}
    )

    await generate_schema_for_client(Tortoise.get_connection("default"), safe=True)

``generate_schema_for_client(client, safe)``
    * ``client`` – same as above.
    * ``safe`` – same meaning as above.

The function internally calls ``get_schema_sql``, logs the generated SQL at DEBUG level, and then executes it against the database in a single transaction.

--------------------------------------------------
Typical usage patterns
--------------------------------------------------

Development / testing
    .. code-block:: python

        await Tortoise.init(...)
        await generate_schema_for_client(Tortoise.get_connection("default"), safe=True)

CI / migrations
    .. code-block:: python

        await Tortoise.init(...)
        sql = get_schema_sql(Tortoise.get_connection("default"), safe=False)
        with open("schema.sql", "w") as f:
            f.write(sql)

--------------------------------------------------
Notes
--------------------------------------------------

* The schema generator is backend-specific; the same model definitions will produce PostgreSQL, SQLite, or MySQL compatible DDL automatically.
* If no models are registered for a connection, the generated SQL will be an empty string.
* DDL is executed in the order required by foreign-key dependencies, so circular dependencies are resolved automatically.

.. _config:

Configuration
=============

ASAB applications are configured through an INI-style configuration file and/or environment variables.
The configuration is available at runtime via the global object ``asab.Config`` (an instance of ``ConfigParser``).

.. code-block:: python

    my_conf_value = asab.Config['section_name']['key']

Configuration file
------------------

Location
~~~~~~~~

The configuration file is looked up in the following order:

1. Path specified in the environment variable ``ASAB_CONFIG``.
2. If the variable is not set, no file is loaded unless explicitly provided.

Include directive
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

Other files can be included from the main configuration file with the special key ``include`` in the ``[general]`` section:

.. code-block:: ini

    [general]
    include = /etc/myapp/*.conf
              /opt/myapp/extra.conf

- Wildcards (``*``, ``?``) are expanded with ``glob``.
- Includes are processed recursively; cyclic includes are detected and skipped.
- Environment variables (``$VAR`` or ``${VAR}``) are expanded.
- The pseudo-variable ``${THIS_DIR}`` expands to the directory of the file currently being read.

ZooKeeper includes
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

Configuration fragments can also be stored in Apache ZooKeeper and pulled at start-up:

.. code-block:: ini

    [general]
    include = zookeeper://zk1:2181,zk2:2181,zk3:2181/asab/etc/zk-site.conf

Supported formats: ``.conf`` (plain INI), ``.json``, ``.yaml``.

Environment variable expansion
------------------------------

All configuration values are processed for environment variable substitution:

.. code-block:: ini

    [paths]
    log_dir = ${HOME}/logs
    cache_dir = ${THIS_DIR}/cache

Default sections and keys
-------------------------

The following sections and keys are pre-defined by ASAB.  You can override any of them in your configuration file.

[general]
~~~~~~~~~
.. list-table::
   :header-rows: 1

   * - Key
     - Default
     - Description
   * - ``config_file``
     - ``$ASAB_CONFIG``
     - Path to the main configuration file.
   * - ``tick_period``
     - ``1``
     - Main event-loop tick period in seconds.
   * - ``var_dir``
     - ``~/.${APPNAME}``
     - Base directory for variable application data.
   * - ``changelog``
     - *(empty)*
     - Path to changelog file (used by documentation generator).
   * - ``manifest``
     - *(empty)*
     - Path to manifest file (used by documentation generator).
   * - ``pidfile``
     - ``!``
     - PID file location.  ``!`` expands to a platform-specific default.
   * - ``working_dir``
     - ``.``
     - Working directory after daemonization.
   * - ``uid``
     - *(empty)*
     - User name/UID to switch to after daemonization.
   * - ``gid``
     - *(empty)*
     - Group name/GID to switch to after daemonization.

[asab:metrics]
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
.. list-table::
   :header-rows: 1

   * - Key
     - Default
     - Description
   * - ``native_metrics``
     - ``true``
     - Enable built-in metrics collection.
   * - ``web_requests_metrics``
     - ``false``
     - Enable per-request metrics for the web server.
   * - ``expiration``
     - ``60``
     - Time-to-live for metrics in seconds.

[asab:doc]
~~~~~~~~~~
.. list-table::
   :header-rows: 1

   * - Key
     - Default
     - Description
   * - ``default_route_tag``
     - ``module_name``
     - Default tag used for grouping API routes in documentation.

[logging]

   * - Key

   * - ``app_name``

     - Human-readable application name in logs.
   * - ``sd_id``
     - ``sd``
     - Structured-data ID for RFC 5424 syslog messages.
   * - ``level``
     - ``NOTICE``
     - Global log level (DEBUG, INFO, NOTICE, WARNING, ERROR, CRITICAL).

[passwords]
~~~~~~~~~~~
Dedicated section for storing secrets.  Values here are hidden from the default REST API.

.. code-block:: ini

    [passwords]
    kafka_password = s3cr3t

    [connection:KafkaConnection]
    password = ${passwords:kafka_password}

[housekeeping]
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
.. list-table::
   :header-rows: 1

   * - Key
     - Default
     - Description
   * - ``at``
     - ``03:00``
     - Time of day when housekeeping tasks run (HH:MM).
   * - ``limit``
     - ``05:00``
     - Latest allowed finish time (HH:MM).
   * - ``run_at_startup``
     - ``no``
     - Run housekeeping immediately after start.

[zookeeper]
~~~~~~~~~~~
Only present when the environment variable ``ASAB_ZOOKEEPER_SERVERS`` is defined.

.. list-table::
   :header-rows: 1

   * - Key
     - Default
     - Description
   * - ``servers``
     - ``$ASAB_ZOOKEEPER_SERVERS``
     - Comma-separated list of ZooKeeper nodes ``host:port``.

Helper methods
--------------

``Config.getseconds(section, option)``
    Parse a human-readable time string (``1d 2h 3m 4s``) into seconds.

``Config.geturl(section, option, scheme='https')``
    Validate and normalize a URL, optionally enforcing a scheme.

``Config.getmultiline(section, option)``
    Split a whitespace-separated list into a Python list of strings.

``Config.get_config_contents_list()``
    Return the raw contents and names of all configuration files/ZooKeeper nodes that were loaded (useful for debugging).

Configurable objects
--------------------

Any class that inherits from ``asab.Configurable`` can automatically load its attributes from a configuration section.

.. code-block:: python

    class MyService(asab.Configurable):

        ConfigDefaults = {
            "retry_count": 3,
            "timeout": "10s",
        }

        def __init__(self, app, service_name):
            super().__init__(config_section_name=service_name)
            self.RetryCount = self.Config.getint("retry_count")
            self.Timeout = self.Config.getseconds("timeout")

The configuration section ``[MyService]`` can now override the defaults:

.. code-block:: ini

    [MyService]
    retry_count = 5
    timeout = 30s
results.reference:
Configuration

The configuration is provided by Config object which is a singleton. It
means that you can access Config from any place of your code, without
need of explicit initialisation.

    import asab

    # Initialize application object and hence the configuration
    app = asab.Application()

    # Access configuration values anywhere
    my_conf_value = asab.Config['section_name']['key1']

Based on ConfigParser

The Config is inherited from Python Standard Library
configparser.ConfigParser class. which implements a basic configuration
language which provides a structure similar to what’s found in Microsoft
Windows INI files.

Example of the configuration file:

    [bitbucket.org]
    User = hg

    [topsecret.server.com]
    Port = 50022
    ForwardX11 = no

And this is how you access configuration values:

    >>> asab.Config['topsecret.server.com']['ForwardX11']
    'no'

Multiline configuration entry

A multiline configuration entries are supported. An example:

    [section]
    key=
      line1
      line2
      line3
    another_key=foo

Automatic load of configuration

If a configuration file name is specified, the configuration is
automatically loaded from a configuration file during initialiation time
of Application. The configuration file name can be specified by one of
-c command-line argument (1), ASAB_CONFIG environment variable (2) or
config [general] config_file default value (3).

    ./sample_app.py -c ./etc/sample.conf

Including other configuration files

You can specify one or more additional configuration files that are
loaded and merged from an main configuration file. It is done by
[general] include configuration value. Multiple paths are separated by
os.pathsep (: on Unix). The path can be specified as a glob (e.g. use
of * and ? wildcard characters), it will be expanded by glob module from
Python Standard Library. Included configuration files may not exists,
this situation is silently ignored.

    [general]
    include=./etc/site.conf:./etc/site.d/*.conf

You can also use a multiline configuration entry:

    [general]
    include=
        ./etc/site.conf
        ./etc/site.d/*.conf

Configuration default values

This is how you can extend configuration default values:

    asab.Config.add_defaults(
        {
            'section_name': {
                'key1': 'value',
                'key2': 'another value'
            },
            'other_section': {
                'key3': 'value',
            },
        }
    )

Only simple types (string, int and float) are allowed in the
configuration values. Don't use complex types such as lists,
dictionaries or objects because these are impossible to provide via
configuration files etc.

Environment variables in configration

Environment variables found in values are automatically expanded.

    [section_name]
    persistent_dir=${HOME}/.myapp/

    >>> asab.Config['section_name']['persistent_dir']
    '/home/user/.myapp/'

There is a special environment variable ${THIS_DIR} that is expanded to
a directory that contains a current configuration file. It is useful in
complex configurations that utilizes included configuration files etc.

    [section_name]
    my_file=${THIS_DIR}/my_file.txt

Another environment variable ${HOSTNAME} contains the application
hostname to be used f. e. in logging file path.

    [section_name]
    my_file=${THIS_DIR}/${HOSTNAME}/my_file.txt

Passwords in configration

[passwords] section in the configuration serves to securely store
passwords, which are then not shown publicly in the default API config
endpoint's output.

It is convenient for the user to store passwords at one place, so that
they are not repeated in many sections of the config file(s).

Usage is as follows:

    [connection:KafkaConnection]
    password=${passwords:kafka_password}

    [passwords]
    kafka_password=<MY_SECRET_PASSWORD>

Obtaining seconds

The seconds can be obtained using getseconds() method for values with
different time units specified in the configuration:

    [sleep]
    sleep_time=5.2s
    another_sleep_time=10d

The available units are:

  -   y ... years
  -   M ... months
  -   w ... weeks
  -   d ... days
  -   h ... hours
  -   m ... minutes
  -   s ... seconds
  -   ms .. miliseconds

If no unit is specified, float of seconds is expected.

The obtainment of the second value in the code can be achieved in two
ways:

    self.SleepTime = asab.Config["sleep"].getseconds("sleep_time")
    self.AnotherSleepTime = asab.Config.getseconds("sleep", "another_sleep_time")

Obtaining URLs

A URL can be obtained using a geturl() method that takes the URL from
the config and removes leading and trailing whitespaces and trailing
backslashes.

There is an optional parameter called scheme that can have any URL
scheme like http, https, mongodb etc. Setting it to None, scheme
validation gets bypassed.

Setting the scheme parameter to the same scheme as in the config, it
will return the URL. If it's not the same it will raise an error.

There are two ways of obtaining the URL:

    asab.Config["urls"].geturl("teskalabs", scheme="https")
    asab.Config.geturl("urls", "github", scheme=None)

Example:

    >>> asab.Config["urls"].geturl("teskalabs", scheme="https")
        'https://www.teskalabs.com'

For reference this would be the configuration file:

    [urls]
    teskalabs=https://www.teskalabs.com/
    github=github.com

.. _library:

Library
=======

The **Library** module provides pluggable storage backends for a hierarchical
collection of configuration files, templates, schemas and other assets that an
ASAB application may need at runtime.

It exposes a unified API for listing and reading items regardless of the actual
storage technology (Azure Blob Storage, ZooKeeper, local file-system, …).

.. contents::
   :local:
   :depth: 2


Core concepts
-------------

LibraryItem
~~~~~~~~~~~

A lightweight descriptor returned by every provider when listing a path.

.. code-block:: python

   LibraryItem(
       name="/folder/file.yaml",
       type="item",          # or "dir"
       layer=10,             # numeric priority used when merging
       providers=[provider]  # list of providers that own the item
   )

Layer
~~~~~

Providers are stacked in ascending *layer* order.  
If the same logical path exists in multiple providers, the one with the
highest layer wins.  This allows e.g. a read-only system library to be
shadowed by a deployment-specific overlay.

Provider registry
-----------------

A provider is registered simply by placing a class that inherits from
``LibraryProviderABC`` in the ``asab.library.providers`` package.  The
configuration key ``[library] providers`` contains a whitespace- or
newline-separated list of URLs; each URL scheme is mapped to the
corresponding provider.

Example:

.. code-block:: ini

   [library]
   providers:
       zk:///library
       azure+https://acme.blob.core.windows.net/configs?sv=…
       file:///opt/myapp/library


Built-in providers
------------------

Azure Blob Storage – ``azure+https://…``
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

``AzureStorageLibraryProvider`` connects to a Microsoft Azure Storage
container and exposes its blobs as library items.

Configuration
^^^^^^^^^^^^^

* **Minimal public container**

  .. code-block:: ini

     [library]
     providers:
         azure+https://ACCOUNT.blob.core.windows.net/CONTAINER

* **Private container with SAS token**

  .. code-block:: ini

     [library]
     providers:
         azure+https://ACCOUNT.blob.core.windows.net/CONTAINER?sv=2020-10-02&si=POLICY&sr=c&sig=…

Optional cache
^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

.. code-block:: ini

   [library]
   azure_cache=true     # or an absolute path, or "false" to disable

When enabled, blobs are cached locally and re-validated with ETags, saving
bandwidth and latency.

ZooKeeper – ``zk://…``
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

``ZooKeeperLibraryProvider`` treats a ZooKeeper sub-tree as a file-system.

Configuration variants
^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

1. **Everything from the** ``[zookeeper]`` **section**

   .. code-block:: ini

      [zookeeper]
      servers=zoo1:2181,zoo2:2181,zoo3:2181
      path=/library

      [library]
      providers:
          zk://

2. **Servers from config, path from URL**

   .. code-block:: ini

      [library]
      providers:
          zk:///library

3. **Fully specified in URL**

   .. code-block:: ini

      [library]
      providers:
          zk://zoo1:2181,zoo2:2181/library

4. **Merged path** (``./`` suffix)

   .. code-block:: ini

      [zookeeper]
      path=/base
      [library]
      providers:
          zk://./overlay

   Resulting path: ``/base/overlay``

Change detection
^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

The provider watches the znode ``/.version.yaml`` (a simple integer counter)
and also computes recursive SHA-1 digests of subscribed directories every
minute.  Applications can subscribe to ``Library.change!`` events to reload
configuration on the fly.

API reference
-------------

.. autoclass:: asab.library.providers.abc.LibraryProviderABC
   :members: list, read, subscribe

.. autoclass:: asab.library.providers.azure.AzureStorageLibraryProvider
   :members:

.. autoclass:: asab.library.providers.zookeeper.ZooKeeperLibraryProvider
   :members:

.. autoclass:: asab.library.item.LibraryItem
   :members:
results.reference:
Library

The ASAB Library (asab.library) is a concept of the shared data content
across microservices in the cluster. The asab.library provides a
read-only interface for listing and reading this content. The library
can also notify the ASAB microservice about changes, eg. for automated
update/reload.

There is a companion microservice asab-library that can be used for
management and editation of the library content. The asab.library can
however operate without asab-library microservice.

Library structure

The library content is organized in simplified filesystem manner, with
directories and files.

Example of the library structure:

    + /folder1/
      - /folder1/item1.yaml
      - /folder1/item2.json
    + /folder2/
      - /folder2/item3.yaml
      + /folder2folder2.3/
        - /folder2/folder2.3/item4.json

Library path rules

-   Any path must start with /, including the root path (/).
-   The folder path must end with /.
-   The item path must end with extension (eg. .json).

Library service

LibraryService

Example of the use:

    import asab

    class MyApplication(asab.Application):

        def __init__(self):
            super().__init__()

            # Initialize the library service 
            self.LibraryService = asab.library.LibraryService(self, "LibraryService")
            self.PubSub.subscribe("Library.ready!", self.on_library_ready)

        async def on_library_ready(self, event_name, library):
            print("# Library\n")

            for item in await self.LibraryService.list("", recursive=True):
                print(" *", item)
                if item.type == 'item':
                    itemio = await self.LibraryService.read(item.name)
                    if itemio is not None:
                        with itemio:
                            content = itemio.read()
                            print("  - content: {} bytes".format(len(content)))
                    else:
                        print("  - (DISABLED)")

Providers

The library can be configured to work with following "backends" (aka
providers):

Git repository

Connection to git repositories requires pygit2 library to be installed.

Example of configuration:

    [library]
    providers: git+https://github.com/john/awesome_project.git

Functionality

The git provider clones the repository into a temporary directory and
then uses the File System Provider to read the files from it. The
default path for the cloned repository is /tmp/asab.library.git/ and it
can be changed manually:

    [library:git]
    repodir=path/to/repository/cache

Deploy tokens in GitLab

GitLab uses deploy tokens to enable authentication of deployment tasks,
independent of a user account. A deploy token is an SSH key that grants
access to a single repository. The public part of the key is attached
directly to the repository instead of a personal account, and the
private part of the key remains on the server. It is the preferred
preferred way over changing local SSH settings.

If you want to create a deploy token for your GitLab repository, follow
these steps from the manual:

1.  Go to Settings > Repository > Deploy tokens section in your
    repository. (Note that you have to possess "Maintainer" or "Owner"
    role for the repository.)
2.  Expand the "Deploy tokens" section. The list of current Active
    Deploy Tokens will be displayed.
3.  Complete the fields and scopes. We recommend to specify custom
    "username", as you will need it later for the url in configuration.
4.  Record the deploy token's values before leaving or refreshing the
    page! After that, you cannot access it again.

After the deploy token is created, use the URL for repository in the
following format:

    https://<username>:<deploy_token>@gitlab.example.com/john/awesome_project.git

Layers

The library content can be organized into unlimmited number of layers.
Each layer is represented by a provider with a specific configuration.

Library configuration

Example:

    [library]
    providers:
        provider+1://...
        provider+2://...
        provider+3://...
